title: Eviction-batcher slab trace dive
linked_artifacts: Confluence: Serving Runtime Traces - slab eviction notes (page id 99234)
content:
Summary:
This note captures an investigation into an emergent high-p99 observed on the hosted inference fleet over the last week. The pattern shows large tail latency spikes correlated with a particular class of traces that experience an eviction from the in-node KV slab (approx 4–6% of requests in the sample window). We instrumented traces at token granularity and combined eBPF TCP timing hooks + runtime stage annotations to reconstruct per-stage breakdowns and cohort behavior.

Context & why this matters:
- Customer-facing SLA: target p99 < 800ms for short chat requests (prompt+<64 tokens). Observed p99 rose to ~1.6s for the cohort below.
- Impact: bursty tail increases token cost (retries/backoff) and degrades UX for synchronous clients.
- Suspected mechanism: slab eviction causes cache miss storms which trigger additional KV lookups + model cold-path interactions + extended batching wait windows.

Data & sample window:
- Window: 2025-02-10 00:00 to 2025-02-11 23:59 (48 hours)
- Hosts sampled: 1200 nodes across us-west-2 (g5-like) serving model family m-opti-7B variants
- Requests analyzed: 2.4M total; cohort of interest (eviction-on-hit) = 98k (4.1%)
- Trace capture: full-span tracing on 5% of requests, token-level spans for model forward and kv-cache ops on flagged nodes.

Methodology:
1) Group traces by "Eviction Flag" which we add to runtime span when a slab eviction was observed within the request lifecycle (eviction event timestamped).
2) Compute per-stage quantiles (p50/p95/p99) for stages: tokenization, routing, prebatch, batch-wait, model-forward, kv-lookup(s), postprocess, egress.
3) Inspect per-trace flame slices for co-occurring patterns (e.g., repeated kv retries, backpressure spikes).
4) Compare to matched-control traces (same route, approx same seq_len distribution) without eviction.

Key aggregate numbers (cohort = short-chat requests <64 tokens):
- Control cohort (no-evict): p50=165ms, p95=480ms, p99=810ms
- Eviction cohort: p50=220ms, p95=980ms, p99=1620ms
- Delta at p99: +810ms (eviction cohort vs control)

Per-stage median and tail summary (eviction cohort / control cohort):
- Tokenization: 6ms / 5ms (p50), p95 10ms / 9ms, p99 14ms / 12ms
- Routing & auth: 9ms / 8ms (p50), p95 18ms / 17ms, p99 40ms / 22ms
- Prebatch work (serialization checks + KV check): 18ms / 12ms (p50), p95 70ms / 36ms, p99 220ms / 90ms
- Batch-wait (time spent queued waiting for a batch to form): 240ms / 80ms (p50), p95 680ms / 220ms, p99 1320ms / 420ms
- Model-forward (actual matmul/ops): 140ms / 135ms (p50), p95 160ms / 150ms, p99 210ms / 195ms
- KV lookups (additional rounds due to eviction): 92ms / 18ms (p50), p95 240ms / 48ms, p99 520ms / 120ms
- Postprocess & safety checks: 25ms / 24ms (p50), p95 38ms / 36ms, p99 60ms / 48ms
- Egress & network: 12ms / 10ms (p50), p95 28ms / 22ms, p99 48ms / 36ms

Interpretation / pattern notes:
- The dominant contributors to the increased tail are batch-wait and additional KV lookup rounds. Model-forward time is relatively stable across cohorts, which rules out model compute variability as the main cause.
- Eviction events often coincide with ephemeral microbursts of allocations inside the slab allocator; when an eviction occurs it triggers synchronous fallback code path that issues a second round of KV misses + small re-routes.
- Those fallback KV rounds do two things: (a) increase per-request critical path by ~60–400ms depending on network hops, (b) increase the window before request reaches the batching stage (prebatch + kv retries), causing it to miss its original micro-batch and be queued alone or with a smaller batch -> batch-wait multiplies.
- We see a non-linear effect: a single eviction in a node can cause 10x increase in local batch-wait because several requests become desynchronized at the same time.

Representative trace excerpts (abbreviated):
- trace_id: 2f9a3b1c - seq_len=38 - eviction_detected=true
  - tokenize: 6ms
  - routing: 12ms
  - prebatch(kv-check): 18ms
  - kv-miss -> fallback fetch: 110ms
  - kv-retry roundtrip: 82ms
  - batch-wait (missed original batch): 540ms
  - model-forward: 190ms
  - postprocess: 30ms
  - total: ~988ms (this was around p95 for the eviction cohort)

- trace_id: a7d13fa0 - seq_len=10 - eviction_detected=true
  - tokenization: 5ms
  - prebatch: 22ms (kv-check + small re-serialize)
  - kv-fallback fetch: 210ms
  - batch-wait: 1200ms (single-shot batch due to desynch)
  - model-forward: 150ms
  - total: ~1587ms (p99 region)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Slab allocator eviction frequency increases under moderate fragmentation -> triggers fallback path in >4% of requests. Reducing eviction rate should compress p99.
2) Fallback KV fetch code path is synchronous and not coalesced; turning it into an async prefetch or coalesced path would reduce both kv time and batch desync.
3) Batcher admission logic is sensitive to small shifts in arrival time; we can reduce penalty if we add a short "re-bucket" window for requests that re-enter batchable path within X ms of initial admission.
4) Network variance for fallback lookup is amplified by cross-az hops during eviction storms; pin fallbacks to local memory/replica when possible.

Quick experiments we ran (results):
- Experiment A: Increase slab per-shard reserve by 10% on a canary subset (10 hosts) for 36 hours.
  - Result: eviction events on canary fell from 4.3% -> 0.9%. p99 for canary fell to ~780ms (control region 1.6s). No measurable CPU or memory pressure increase beyond acceptable bounds.
- Experiment B: Convert fallback KV fetch to use a coalescing ticket (micro-batcher) in front of remote fetch.
  - Result (lab): single-host microbench showed ~45% reduction in kv latency tail (p99->p99.5) and reduced number of simultaneous batch desyncs. Not yet deployed to fleet.
- Experiment C: Reduce max-batch-wait threshold (trade throughput for latency) on short-chat route by 30ms.
  - Result: reduced batch-wait p95 by ~12% but throughput (tokens/sec) dropped ~2.4%. Small positive UX improvement but cost tradeoff.

Actionable next steps (short-term):
- Roll out slab reserve increase to 20% on 5% of fleet (owner: Mateo, ETA: 2025-03-04) and monitor eviction flag rate + p99.
- Implement coalesced fallback fetch in GH PR and run staged canary (owner: Ethan, PR link in linked_artifacts). Target review by 2025-03-10.
- Add an instrumentation metric (eviction_session_id) surfaced to Console per-host to correlate eviction storms with batch scheduling windows (owner: Priya, ETA: 2025-03-05).
- Add a one-off batcher heuristic: when request experiences KV-fallback inside prebatch, mark it as "re-bucketable" for 120ms to allow it to join the next short window (owner: Lina, spike due 2025-03-07).

Longer-term considerations:
- Consider redesigning in-node slab eviction policy to prefer ephemeral buffers (short lived) over long-lived feature caches under bursty patterns. Requires allocator-level changes and testing.
- Evaluate persistent per-host hot-key prefetching for top-N keys in the slab to reduce fallback fetches for popular prompts.
- Revisit admission control for the batcher to better tolerate a small number of re-sequenced tokens without creating single-shot batches.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How common are cross-az network fallbacks during eviction? Need per-request AZ tags + fallback routing trace to confirm.
- Can we safely co-locate fallback fetch replies in the same worker thread to prevent preemption? Might impact CPU tail.
- Are there specific prompt patterns that disproportionately trigger eviction (large embeddings, few heavy cached keys)? Need content-level telemetry (masked) to analyze.

Appendix: quick commands used to assemble traces
- Trace query (example):
  curl -sS 'https://trace-api/internal/query' -d '{"time_range":"2025-02-10/2025-02-11","filter":"eviction_flag=true AND model=m-opti-7B"}' | jq '.' > eviction_traces.json
- Per-stage aggregation snippet (one-liner):
  jq -r '.spans[] | select(.stage) | [.trace_id, .stage, .duration_ms] | @tsv' eviction_traces.json | sort -k3 -n | scripts/stage-quantiles.py

Owners & next check-in:
- Primary owner for follow-ups: Priya Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Secondary owners: Mateo Garcia (allocator), Ethan Brooks (kv/cache), Lina Zhou (batcher)
- Next sync: 2025-03-06, retro + canary rollout review.

Notes to self:
- Exported detailed flamegraphs into /mnt/observation/eviction-flames/ -- useful for the PR description.
- Capture a short 10m pprof of the coalescing micro-batcher lab to attach to the GH PR.

End of note.
